**Death and the King's Horseman**
Soyinka's best-known play (1975), based on a real 1946 incident in the Yoruba city of Oyo, Nigeria. Elesin Oba, the King's Horseman, is supposed to commit ritual suicide after the king's death so he can follow his master into the afterlife. The British District Officer Simon Pilkings arrests him to stop it. Soyinka, the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature (1986), is most often clued through this play.

**Olunde**
Elesin's eldest son, who has been studying medicine in England. He returns for the ritual and tells Jane Pilkings that the British "have no respect for what you do not understand." After his father's suicide is prevented, Olunde kills himself in Elesin's place. When his wrapped body is brought to his chained father, Elesin strangles himself with his chains.

**The "Not-I" bird and the Praise-Singer**
At the start of Death and the King's Horseman, Elesin moves through the market with his Praise-Singer (Olohun-iyo) and drummer and tells the tale of the Not-I bird. In the tale, every creature that Death visits cries "Not I" to escape it, while Elesin boasts that he will not be afraid. The Praise-Singer teases him for enjoying the admiration of the market women.

**Iyaloja and Elesin's bride**
Iyaloja, the "mother" of the market women, lets Elesin marry a beautiful young girl on his final day, even though she is engaged to Iyaloja's own son. Elesin's distraction by this worldly pleasure is part of why he fails to complete the ritual, and Iyaloja later scorns him for his failure.

**The egungun costume and Soyinka's preface**
Simon and Jane Pilkings put on egungun costumes, sacred Yoruba ancestral masquerade robes, for a colonial fancy-dress ball, which horrifies the Nigerian police sergeant Amusa. Soyinka's preface warns against the "reductionist tendency" of reading the play as a simple "clash of cultures" and asks directors to bring out its "threnodic essence," meaning its mourning quality.

**The Lion and the Jewel**
Soyinka's 1959 comedy set in the Yoruba village of Ilujinle. The village beauty Sidi (the "Jewel") is courted by the young, Westernized schoolteacher Lakunle and by the cunning old chief Baroka (the "Lion"). Baroka tricks and seduces her, and at the end Sidi chooses to marry him and join his harem, leaving Lakunle devastated.

**Lakunle**
The comic schoolteacher in The Lion and the Jewel, who wears an old, too-small Western suit and talks in pompous English he learned from a "Shorter Companion Dictionary." He tells Sidi that women are the weaker sex because their brains are smaller, and he refuses to pay her traditional bride price, calling it a savage custom.

**The Stranger's photographs and the "Dance of the Lost Traveller"**
In The Lion and the Jewel, a photographer from Lagos once came to the village and published pictures of Sidi in a magazine, which has made her vain. The villagers act out his arrival in the "Dance of the Lost Traveller": girls play his broken-down motor car, and they mock his motorbike as "the devil's own horse" and his camera as "the one-eyed box." Lakunle is made to play the stranger before being excused to go teach his Primary Four geography class.

**Baroka's stamp machine and "I do not hate progress"**
To seduce Sidi, Baroka shows her a stamp-printing machine and promises to put her picture on postage stamps. He claims he does "not hate progress, only its nature, which makes all roofs and faces look the same." Baroka is first seen having a favorite wife pluck the hairs from his armpits, and his senior wife Sadiku is tricked into thinking he has become impotent.

**Kongi's Harvest**
A 1965 satire of African dictatorship. Kongi, the tyrant of the fictional state of Isma, wants the deposed traditional king Oba Danlola to hand him the ceremonial new yam at the harvest festival so that his power will look legitimate. Danlola's nephew Daodu and his lover Segi plot against Kongi, and at the climax Kongi is presented with the severed head of Segi's father instead of a yam.

**A Dance of the Forests**
A play written for Nigerian independence in 1960. The living hold a Gathering of the Tribes expecting to welcome illustrious ancestors, but the Forest Head and his servant Aroni instead summon a Dead Man and a Dead Woman, who come to "take their case" against the past. The Dead Man turns out to have been a warrior sold into slavery for a flask of rum. The trickster spirit Eshuoro also disrupts the gathering.

**The Trials of Brother Jero**
A comedy about Brother Jeroboam, a fraudulent prophet who preaches on Bar Beach in Lagos. He manipulates his follower Chume and at first forbids him to beat his nagging wife Amope, to whom Jero owes money, then gives him permission. The sequel, Jero's Metamorphosis, sees Jero scheming against rival preachers like Shadrach.

**The Interpreters**
Soyinka's first novel (1965), about a group of young Nigerian intellectuals who have come home after studying abroad and try to make sense of post-independence society. They include the engineer turned sculptor Sekoni, the journalist Sagoe, and the painter Kola. His second novel is Season of Anomy.

**Chronicles from the Land of the Happiest People on Earth**
Soyinka's 2021 satirical novel about Nigerian corruption. The surgeon Dr. Menka discovers a racket that steals human body parts from his hospital for ritual use. His friend Duyole Pitan-Payne, an engineer about to take a United Nations post, is killed by a bomb.

**The Man Died and political imprisonment**
A prison memoir from Soyinka's nearly two years of detention, much of it in solitary confinement, during the Nigerian Civil War for trying to broker peace with Biafra. After his release, he went into exile and edited the magazine Transition. He also adapted Euripides as The Bacchae of Euripides.
